blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a clever and surprisingly effective approach to combating voice spam using a simple chatbot named Lenny. Despite lacking AI or speech recognition, Lenny—a pre-recorded voice bot—keeps telemarketers and scammers engaged for an average of over 10 minutes per call by leveraging principles from Conversation Analysis (CA). The bot’s success stems from its adherence to adjacency pairs (e.g., question-answer sequences) and turn-taking norms, which exploit the predictable scripts spammers follow. The paper analyzes 200 calls from Lenny’s public archive, showing that 72% of conversations repeat Lenny’s script multiple times, and only 5% of spammers realize they’re talking to a bot. Colyer emphasizes Lenny’s simplicity and the broader applicability of CA techniques for designing interactive systems.
paper_title: Using chatbots against voice spam: analyzing Lenny's effectiveness
paper_abstract: A new countermeasure recently appeared to fight back against unwanted phone calls (such as, telemarketing, survey or scam calls), which consists in connecting back the telemarketer with a phone bot (“robocallee”) which mimics a real persona. Lenny is such a bot (a computer program) which plays a set of pre-recorded voice messages to interact with the spammers. Although not based on any sophisticated artificial intelligence, Lenny is surprisingly effective in keeping the conversation going for tens of minutes. Moreover, it is clearly recognized as a bot in only 5% of the calls recorded in our dataset. In this paper, we try to understand why Lenny is so successful in dealing with spam calls. To this end, we analyze the recorded conversations of Lenny with various types of spammers. Among 487 publicly available call recordings, we select 200 calls and transcribe them using a commercial service. With this dataset, we first explore the spam ecosystem captured by this chatbot, presenting several statistics on Lenny’s interaction with spammers. Then, we use conversation analysis to understand how Lenny is adjusted with the sequential context of such spam calls, keeping a natural flow of conversation. Finally, we discuss a range of research and design issues to gain a better understanding of chatbot conversations and to improve their efficiency.
